payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
IFPI published five baseline practices for music distributors on September 14 and asked the industry to commit to them. The document contains one penalty clause, and it points at the customer.

The only penalty points at the uploader

The Streaming Integrity Initiative sets out five baseline practices for distributors.

The five practices

Verify. Establish the identity and legitimacy of the customer through Know Your Customer checks before distributing anything.

Vet. Filter content against third party rights, and implement measures to identify AI-generated material and protect voice, name, image and likeness.

Act. Detect and investigate suspected fraud, and operate a penalty system that bans the customer across all platforms after repeated violations.

Share. Run cross-partner checks and share high-confidence indicators where data protection law permits it.

Measure. Track the efficacy of those measures on a regular basis and make reasonable updates.

That is the only place in the document where a consequence attaches to anyone, and it attaches to the person uploading.

Nothing in the text describes what follows for a distributor that adds its name and implements none of the five. There is no audit provision, no reporting cadence, no review, and no procedure for removing a name once it appears. The verbs governing the distributor's own conduct are should and urge.

Measurement with no recipient

The fifth practice asks distributors to track the efficacy of their measures on a regular basis and to make reasonable updates based on their own data. There is no counterparty anywhere in that sentence. The distributor gathers the data, assesses its own performance against it, and reports the result to nobody.

Robust, effective, reasonable, regular. Each of those does load-bearing work in the document and none of them is defined in it. Compliance ends up self-scored against a standard whose terms the scorer interprets. That separates the claim of compliance from the fact of it, and nothing downstream can detect the gap.

"Compliance ends up self-scored against a standard whose terms the scorer interprets."

From the post above

The fourth practice compounds this. Information sharing is the one commitment whose performance another signatory could observe directly, and it is conditioned on data protection compliance and on arrangements the document neither specifies nor requires anyone to join. A distributor that shares nothing has a reading of the text available in which it shared everything it lawfully could.

The list is doing the verification

The corpus has worked through this shape already at the level of a single upload. A declaration that costs nothing to enter and nothing to support records very little about whoever enters it, and the structure does not change when the party declaring is a company and the field is a press release.

Twenty-four organizations appeared on the participant list at launch. Their presence there was the whole of the public evidence that any of the five practices operates anywhere. Practices that cost nothing to endorse recruit most easily among the distributors already following them, which tells a reader something about the signatories and very little about the rest of the field.

The initiative is right about the position distributors occupy. They are the entry point into the ecosystem, and asking them to establish who is uploading is a reasonable thing to ask. What a KYC check produces at that point is an account of the uploader's identity, held by the distributor. What it adds downstream is permission rather than strength.

The account of the diligence then sits with the same party whose diligence is the question. A sixth practice would not reach that. What is missing is a record of the upload that somebody outside the distributor can check without asking the distributor. Proof of origin written while the work is being made is the one version of that record whose worth does not rest on the good faith of the party being asked about.

References

IFPI. "Streaming Integrity Initiative: Protecting Artists, Songwriters and Fans from Streaming Fraud." 2026. endstreamingfraud.com/streaming-integrity-initiative
payload.title: The measuring is left to the measured
